facts.text: Distributional agreement compares the whole spread of many simulated results with the whole spread of many measured results when repeated runs of the same situation legitimately differ.
facts.quote: Distributional agreement compares the whole spread of many simulated results with the whole spread of many measured results, which is needed when repeated runs of the same situation legitimately differ.

facts.text: Repeated real-site perception trials produce different detections because dust density, target reflectivity, lighting, rain rate, sensor contamination and random software effects vary; comparison should therefore use distributions rather than a single simulated and real run.
facts.quote: Comparing one simulated run with one real run is then meaningless. The right comparison is between distributions: the collection of all outcomes and their spread [Chapter 10].

facts.text: Rail acceptance compares distributions using at least 24 comparisons per quantity across at least 12 track sections, with limits on the set of deviations.
facts.quote: Rail acceptance works this way, with at least 24 comparisons per quantity across at least 12 track sections and limits on the set of deviations.

facts.text: The booklet's layered simulation-assessment scheme places distributional metrics between signal-level accuracy and image similarity.
facts.quote: The booklet's layered scheme places distributional metrics between signal-level accuracy and image similarity [Chapters 6, 10].

facts.text: The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test (KS) compares the largest vertical gap between two cumulative curves: values near 0 indicate nearly alike spreads and values near 1 indicate very different spreads. The passage also describes the test as giving a probability that both sets came from the same source.
facts.quote: Near 0: the two sets are spread almost alike. Near 1: very different. Also gives a probability that both came from the same source.

facts.text: Wasserstein distance (earth mover's distance) measures the work needed to reshape one distribution into another in the units of the quantity; small values indicate similarity. The passage gives 0.3 m of stopping distance as an example of a small distance.
facts.quote: Small, for example 0.3 m of stopping distance: alike. Large: far apart, and the number says by how much.

facts.text: Maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) compares two sets after mapping results into a rich mathematical feature space; 0 means the sets cannot be distinguished and larger values indicate greater differences. MMD works for point clouds and other multi-dimensional data.
facts.quote: 0: the sets cannot be told apart. Larger: more different. Works for point clouds and other multi-dimensional data.

facts.text: Kullback-Leibler divergence (KL) measures the discrepancy between an expected and observed distribution: 0 indicates identical distributions and values grow without limit. KL is not symmetric and is undefined where one distribution assigns zero probability to an outcome produced by the other.
facts.quote: 0: identical. Grows without limit. Not symmetric, and undefined where one distribution gives zero chance to something the other produces.

facts.text: Chamfer distance measures the average nearest-neighbor distance between two point clouds in both directions; small values indicate overlapping clouds and large values indicate different shapes. Chamfer distance ignores whether points are crowded or sparse.
facts.quote: For two point clouds, the average distance from each point to its nearest neighbor in the other cloud, both ways

facts.text: Density-aware Chamfer distance (DCD) corrects Chamfer distance for point density and is bounded between 0 and 1, where 0 means identical and 1 means completely different.
facts.quote: Chamfer distance corrected for point density, bounded between 0 and 1

facts.text: A 2025 study reported an average density-aware Chamfer distance of 0.63 between real and simulated scans; density-aware Chamfer distance tracked perception results best.
facts.quote: Real versus simulated scans averaged 0.63 in a 2025 study, and this metric tracked perception results best.

facts.text: The area validation metric (AVM) measures the area between two cumulative curves in the units of the quantity; small values indicate similarity and large values indicate the approximate error in the model's spread of results.
facts.quote: The area between the two cumulative curves, in the units of the quantity

facts.text: The booklet treats the area validation metric value as model-form uncertainty to add to predictions.
facts.quote: The booklet treats the value as model-form uncertainty to add to predictions.

facts.text: Greater experimental scatter makes the area validation metric smaller and the model appear more valid; the metric can over- or under-compensate when random and knowledge-based uncertainty are mixed.
facts.quote: More experimental scatter makes the area validation metric smaller and the model look "more valid", and it can over- or under-compensate when random and knowledge-based uncertainty are mixed.

facts.text: A radar validation paper evaluated Kullback-Leibler divergence and dismissed the metric for its purpose.
facts.quote: A radar validation paper evaluated KL divergence and dismissed it for its purpose.

facts.text: Point-cloud metrics disagree with one another, making the finding that density-aware Chamfer distance tracked perception best important for metric selection.
facts.quote: Point-cloud metrics disagree with one another, which is why the finding that density-aware Chamfer distance tracked perception best matters [Chapters 6, 10].

facts.text: Because perception in dust, rain and glare is stochastic, the booklet recommends distributional validation quantities including detection probability by condition, range-error distributions and the frequency of model residuals near decision boundaries.
facts.quote: the booklet recommends distributional validation quantities such as detection probability by condition, range-error distributions and the frequency of model residuals near decision boundaries.

facts.text: Whether distributional validation metrics predict safety-relevant perception errors remains uncertain.
facts.quote: Whether these metrics predict safety-relevant perception errors is listed as uncertain [Chapters 6, 10].
